At this time of year, countless resources are mobilized to light up the country with festivities and spectacular fireworks. On this day, “O Canada” congratulates itself. On this day, “O Canada” claims to be a champion of human rights. On this day, “O Canada” proclaims itself a fervent defender of justice. On this day, in Canada, survivors of Indian residential schools are fading away as they wait for the maple sweetness of Lady Justice.
En cette journée, La Converse s’attarde: On this day, La Converse dwells on the quest for justice and reconciliation through the eyes of the soul’s severe burn victims.
<strong>Un témoignage à l’origine de mil: A testimony that led to thousands of complaints
En 2023, nous commémorons également les: In 2023, we are also marking 15 years since the Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement (IRSSA) was put in place. This dark agreement is the outcome of a series of painful events set off by the powerful testimony of Phil Fontaine, former National Chief of the Assembly of First Nations, who courageously shared his experience in residential schools in 1991.
Ce témoignage a provoqué une série de li: That testimony triggered a series of lawsuits against the Canadian government and several of the country’s churches, resulting in 11 class actions and some 15,000 individual complaints up to 2007. The government found itself overwhelmed by the volume of proceedings and decided to set up a process called the “Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) process.” That process was nevertheless criticized for disregarding the important contributions and suggestions that came out of the Exploratory Dialogues held over the years. Indigenous communities, activists and universities saw it as reductive and arduous.
Sous la pression de l’Assemblée des Prem: Under pressure from the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) and other organizations, the government began discussions toward a settlement agreement in June 2005, with the appointment of Frank Iacobucci. To ensure that Indigenous voices were represented at the negotiating table, Phil Fontaine and the AFN filed a class action known as Fontaine v. Canada in August 2005. Negotiations moved quickly because of the political instability stemming from the minority status of Paul Martin’s government. An agreement in principle was reached on November 20, 2005, thanks to Belinda Stronach’s crossing the floor to the Liberals in the House of Commons. Negotiations on the Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement (IRSSA) were finalized in August 2006, and the implementation process was launched in the courts on September 19, 2007.
La CRRPI est donc le fruit d’un accord e: The IRSSA is thus the product of an agreement among lawyers for former students, the Assembly of First Nations, other Indigenous organizations, lawyers for the Churches and the Government of Canada. The Agreement gave rise to the well-known Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada (TRC) as well as two payment systems meant to compensate the victims of these institutions.
Le premier système est le Paiement d’exp: The first system is the Common Experience Payment (CEP), which consists of “a lump sum recognizing the experiences lived in Indian residential schools and their impacts.” The sum acknowledges the suffering and trauma endured by former students.
Le deuxième système est le Processus d’é: The second system is the Independent Assessment Process (IAP), which offers “a non-adversarial, claimant-oriented framework for the out-of-court resolution of claims related to sexual abuse, serious physical abuse and other wrongful acts suffered in Indian residential schools.” The process allows victims to submit their claims and receive fair compensation.
De 2008 à 2012, des milliers de personne: From 2008 to 2012, thousands of people filed compensation claims, seeking recognition of the suffering and injustices endured in residential schools for Indigenous children in Canada. The process was long and arduous, with the last compensation cases recorded in March 2021.
<strong>« Le gouvernement cherche simple: “The government is simply trying to ease its conscience”
Parmi ceux qui ont réalisé ce parcours d: Among those who went through this difficult journey is Anne Rock, whose story carries deep scars. She spent a childhood marked by turmoil at the Catholic school in Uashat mak Mani-utenam, caught in the institution’s clutches for seven long years. She heard about the government’s compensation for former residential school students on a community radio show in 2008.
Arrivée à la fin de ce long et pénible p: At the end of this long and painful process, Anne found herself facing a release she was asked to sign. By signing this document, the survivor could no longer sue the federal government and the church responsible for her suffering in civil court to obtain compensation. She signed in tears. She explains that in that moment, the government officials standing in front of her turned into nuns in her mind. The memories resurfaced, and the faces of those who caused her suffering blended with the faces of those who now claimed to be offering her redress.
Bien que ce processus « lui ait donné un: Although the process “gave her a slap that opened a buried drawer,” Anne couldn’t help feeling immense sadness and anger as she signed the release. She explains that it was as if she were being told bluntly: “You can’t go any further. You can’t sue the priest, or anyone else. Shut your mouth and accept what we’re giving you. We’ll provide you with a lawyer and pretend to help you with these proceedings.”
Aujourd’hui âgée de 63 ans, cette femme: Now 63, this courageous woman speaks with candour. No amount of money will ever truly heal her wounds. “The government is trying to buy us off, thinking that if it hands over a few bills, everything will be wiped away. But no, the frustrations, the anger, they’ll stay rooted in us forever. Even if they gave us millions, the aftermath would remain in our feelings, in our minds and within our families. Everything is broken. These deep wounds, these scars, they’ll never fade,” she says bitterly. “The government is simply trying to ease its conscience,” Anne adds, speaking of this semblance of “reconciliation.”
En repensant à son expérience avec les d: Looking back on her experience with the two payment systems (CEP and IAP), she asks herself a question: “What is the price of a broken life?” Anne Rock questions the very existence of justice. “They destroyed my life, my marriage, my spirit, my identity as an Innu woman. I could have grown up in Nutshimit (the land) and acquired all the skills and knowledge of our ancestors… My children and grandchildren still bear the heavy consequences of these traumas. Lives were broken. No, there was no justice,” she says.
<strong>« On m’a éteinte, et j’ai vu mes: “They put my light out, and I watched my children’s light go out too”
Cette opinion de l’institution de la jus: This view of the justice institution is shared by Anne Rock’s sister, Muriel, who also received compensation under the Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement. “How far have they taken us? Can they even measure the extent of our extinction? Do they really understand what I’m talking about? I’m the one who knows how I was reduced to nothing. They put my light out, and I watched my children’s light go out too,” she says with immense bitterness.
Cette dernière a initialement réagi néga: Muriel initially reacted negatively to the compensation, constantly questioning the value placed on Indigenous suffering. “I thought we were being had. We had to refuse, but we had to do it as a group, as communities. But my colleagues’ reaction was that if we refused, it was over. The government wouldn’t come back to it,” she recounts, her heart heavy with a painful sense of injustice.
Au-delà des démarches administratives ér: Beyond the exhausting administrative steps, the most heart-wrenching part of receiving compensation was reliving, in front of government representatives, the horror she had lived through. “When I started telling my story, I hid my face, the tears ran down, it lasted several minutes,” she says in a broken voice, caught in the turmoil of her dark memories.
Ce sentiment d’impuissance la hante tout: This feeling of powerlessness haunted her throughout the process. For her, it was a lost cause well before the release was signed. Muriel explains that the position of a significant number of people in her community left hardly any room to object to or contest the proposed terms. “People in the communities were in a hurry to get their money. They couldn’t wait. We know the heartbreaking reality of the poverty that plagues our communities. Getting $3,000 is a drop in the bucket in a lifetime of misery. To me, it was like a battle lost in advance, one more wound,” she says with emotion, her voice deeply marked by bitterness. She explains that she eventually gave in and signed because she felt alone, abandoned in the face of a system that didn’t seem to understand her real suffering, her real loss.

Tout comme les sœurs Rock, les frères Ki: Like the Rock sisters, the Kistabish brothers both received compensation for the abuse they suffered at the residential school in Amos (Saint-Marc-de-Figuery).
« L’argent ne guérit pas. » C’est ainsi: “Money doesn’t heal.” That is how Norman Kistabish, former chief of the Abitibiwinni First Nation in Val-d’Or, sums up his experience of the compensation process and the Agreement. Inspired by the courage of his brother and sister, who had launched a lawsuit against the government and the Catholic Church, which ran the Saint-Marc-de-Figuery residential school, he found the courage to speak up himself on March 13, 2005, beginning a conversation with his lawyer that would last more than 12 hours. It was the first time he had told of the horrors he had lived through. The more he talked, the more his pain rose to the surface.
Norman Kistabish considère son engagemen: Norman Kistabish considers his involvement in the legal process to be the start of his healing. As part of the Independent Assessment Process, he recounted the abuse he suffered in residential schools over five hearings. Having received higher financial compensation than most survivors, Norman insists that money cannot heal every wound. In his words, “there was no complete justice, only disappointment and coercion.” That feeling of incompleteness persists, and the void remains all the same.
Mais lorsque nous évoquons la réconcilia: But when we bring up reconciliation, Norman’s face lights up with a gentle, resolute smile. He explains that his own reconciliation began well before the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. “It started at home, among us,” he says with a glint of pride in his eyes. It was within his own family, among his friends, his community, his woods, his land that he was able to change the course of his life. “I had passed a path of substance use on to my children, but now I’m a true survivor, a fighter, in my search for well-being,” he tells us. Sitting in front of the soft flames of his candles, the 68-year-old Elder leaves us with this message: “How do you know you’ve had justice? For now, I consider that it’s my healing.”
« On est loin en <em>sacrament</em>, on: “We’re goddamn far from it, we’re light-years away from reconciliation,” says Ejinagosi Kistabish. “People always talk about healing, well, healing isn’t happening. It’s a complex concept, it’s not a goal in itself. Healing is a journey. It’s painful, we mustn’t forget that – it’s for life, for the rest of our lives, that we have to learn to live with this, to cope with it every day, relentlessly,” he continues in an emotional voice.
Après un moment de recueillement, Ejinag: After a moment of reflection, Ejinagosi asks us in a compassionate tone: “Have you ever walked through the doors of the burn hospital in Quebec City?” Then, sinking back into his memories, he goes on: “I went there 20 or 30 years ago. I visited that hospital because I wanted to know whether it was possible to heal from severe burns. As soon as I arrived, I understood right away that I was in the same situation as the burn victims, both physically and mentally. The patients in that hospital don’t suffer only in their physical appearance; what hurts is also in their heads, in their minds. Their bodies are completely mutilated. When you start talking with one of these patients, you understand the pain they feel.”
Ejinagosi, dont le nom signifie « celui: Ejinagosi, whose name means “the one who tells stories,” explains: “That’s why I describe myself as a ‘severe burn victim of the soul.’” In this way he expresses his wish to rename survivors, to call them “the soul’s severe burn victims”, an expression that, according to the man in his seventies, more faithfully captures their experience and the gravity of their invisible scars.
Huit longues années ont passé depuis que: Eight long years have passed since the doors of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission closed. The eldest of the Kistabish brothers, who served as a regional officer, speaks words that come out carefully considered: “No, we can’t claim to have obtained justice, but the TRC did a considerable amount of work. In a flood, you try to foresee everything, but it’s impossible to assess all the damage at once. The TRC did everything that could be done, given the scale of the devastation. You save the ones you can.”
Les Grands brûlés de l’âme, hantés par u: The soul’s severe burn victims, haunted by a perpetual fire, continue to wait impatiently for the caress of Lady Justice. In the shadow of the Canadian flags, administrative red tape deprives many former residential school students of the fruits of their struggle. For now, reconciliation seems to be nothing more than a fleeting echo of fireworks fading into the sky. For their part, the Kistabish brothers and the Rock sisters are focusing on their own healing and on reconciliation within their communities, striving to rekindle the gentle flames that once drove them. They want to pass on their story, in the hope that it will be put to good use to raise awareness among some and inspire resistance in others.
